summary:
ORBITAL is a single-file, client-side Space Mission Design Simulator built with HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no backend or libraries. It teaches spacecraft engineering by making users balance mass, power, data, and cost before launch.

Players pick one of four missions (Earth Watch, Lunar Scout, Mars Pathfinder, Deep Space Survey), a difficulty (Cadet, Pilot, Commander), and solo or 2-4 person crews with defined roles. They then assemble a spacecraft from four instruments, three buses, three power systems, and three communication systems, and choose an orbit, a launcher (400, 900, or 1,800 kg), and a 2-, 5-, or 8-year lifetime.

A central calc() function recalculates the whole design on every change, updating mass (including a 35 kg structural allowance), power demand, science value, data rate, and cost on a live dashboard with progress bars. Four checks (payload, power, downlink, budget) run against limits that tighten with difficulty (budget: $220M Cadet, $180M Pilot, $145M Commander) and show green passes or amber warnings that explain each failure.

Launching runs a scoring model combining mission bonus, instrument science, orbit bonus, lifetime, and failure penalties into a 0-100 score. Outcomes range from Outstanding Engineering to Mission Failure, with an event log, anomalies, and an engineering lesson. Results export as a downloadable .txt mission report. The responsive, space-themed interface works on desktop and mobile.
details:
ORBITAL – Space Mission Design Simulator

Category: Web Development | Space Technology | Interactive Simulation
Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript

Project Overview

ORBITAL is an interactive, web-based educational simulation that introduces users to spacecraft engineering and space mission planning. Users take the role of a mission planner: they design a spacecraft, select scientific instruments, configure power and communication systems, choose an orbital trajectory, and pick a launch vehicle.

How It Works

Users customize mission objectives, spacecraft platforms, instruments, power systems, communication technologies, launch vehicles, and mission duration. From these selections, the simulator automatically calculates:

  • Total spacecraft mass
  • Power demand
  • Scientific data generation
  • Science potential
  • Estimated project cost

Real-time validation then checks whether the configuration meets four essential constraints: payload capacity, power availability, communication capacity, and mission budget.

Key Features

  • Four mission scenarios: Earth observation, lunar exploration, Mars atmosphere study, and deep-space exploration.
  • Difficulty levels that adjust engineering and budget constraints.
  • Team mode with defined roles: Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Flight Director.
  • Mission simulation that produces a performance score, mission outcome, engineering feedback, and a simulated flight event log.
  • Downloadable mission report summarizing the configuration and results.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ORBITAL makes complex mission engineering easier to understand through hands-on experimentation rather than theory alone. Users see how engineering decisions affect one another and learn to balance scientific goals, technical capability, and financial limits. It builds analytical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and resource optimization.

The platform is aimed at students, technology enthusiasts, and beginners interested in space science and aerospace engineering. It raises awareness of spacecraft systems and mission planning, and shows how software can communicate complex scientific ideas.

Technology

Layer

Role

HTML5

Application structure

CSS3

Responsive layouts and space-inspired interface

JavaScript

Interactivity, dynamic calculations, engineering validation, mission scoring, event generation, report downloading

The application runs entirely on the client side, with no backend server or database.

Creative Approach

ORBITAL turns spacecraft engineering into an interactive mission-control experience. Instead of only presenting information, it lets users make engineering decisions and see the consequences immediately. The dark space-themed interface, live resource monitoring, interactive configuration cards, visual validation indicators, and simulated flight results are inspired by real mission-control environments.

Design Considerations

Development took into account instrument capabilities, mass limits, power requirements, communication bandwidth, launch capacity, mission duration, cost, usability, and responsive design. The aim was a balance between scientific performance and engineering feasibility, so users learn that a successful mission depends on more than choosing advanced equipment.

Conclusion

ORBITAL combines web development, engineering concepts, simulation logic, and user experience design in a single interactive platform. It applies programming and problem-solving skills while encouraging curiosity, creativity, and interest in space exploration.
